title: Mesaguamo House / Trópico Arquitectura
text:
Mesaguamo House / Trópico Arquitectura

Located in the mountainous territory of the Cauca River canyon, a few hours from the city of Medellín in the municipality of Támesis, amidst the heat and tropical vegetation, Casa Mesaguamo is calm and slow. It seeks the tranquility of rest, of days that pass without haste. It is an open question between the construction of the intimate landscape and the contemplation of the distant landscape, developing in a succession of patios and living rooms.

title: Jiujiang Ferry Cultural Complex Renovation / TURTLEHILL DESIGN
text:
Jiujiang Ferry Cultural Complex Renovation / TURTLEHILL DESIGN

The abandoned ferry terminal along the Xijiang River in Jiujiang Town, Foshan, once served as a vital dock connecting the riverine islands. With the commissioning of a new terminal, this structure—imbued with memories of waterway transportation—gradually fell into disuse, leaving only a concrete skeleton and steps leading to a decaying pier. Situated at the intersection of a wetland park and a residential area, the site combines ecological sensitivity with community service potential. The design team faced the challenge of transforming this ruin into a multifunctional public space—integrating a bookstore, exhibition hall, café, cultural events, and art performances—within a footprint of less than 150 square meters, while responding to the climatic characteristics of the Pearl River Delta and the region's industrial cultural context.

title: Fenix Art Museum / MAD Architects
text:
Fenix Art Museum / MAD Architects

Fenix is a major new museum that explores migration through the lens of art, opening on a landmark site in Rotterdam's City Harbor, developed by internationally acclaimed architects MAD. With a rapidly expanding collection of historic and contemporary objects, Fenix tells the story of migration through a series of encounters with art, architecture, photography, food, and history. Located in what was once part of the world's largest transshipment warehouse, on a peninsula in Rotterdam's historic port district, Fenix overlooks the docks where millions of migrant journeys began and ended. The monumental 16,000 square meter warehouse has been transformed to become Fenix by MAD Architects with restoration consultation by Bureau Polderman. This is MAD Architects' first commission for a public cultural building in Europe, as well as the first museum to be built by a Chinese firm in Europe. The project was initiated by the Droom en Daad Foundation, founded in 2016. The Foundation is helping redefine Rotterdam for the 21st century - developing new kinds of arts and culture institutions and fostering new creative talent that reflects the city's diversity, its spirit, and its history

title: Kindergarten Aegelmatt / Brandenberger Kloter
text:
Kindergarten Aegelmatt / Brandenberger Kloter

Since the start of the 2026 school year, children in Pratteln, Switzerland, have been learning and playing in a new timber building by Brandenberger Kloter Architekten. Kindergarten Aegelmatt brings a kindergarten and a day-care centre together under one roof. The façades of untreated timber change with the weather, the light and the seasons, making the passing of time visible to the children.

title: Japanese Perspectives
text:
Japanese Perspectives

Japanese Perspectives, published by Distanz Verlag, Berlin, explores architectural responses to resource scarcity, demographic change, and climate adaptation through the lens of contemporary Japan.
Bringing together essays by Japanese architects, selected projects and observations from everyday urban life, the book examines practices of reuse, transformation, and working with existing structures.
The contributions reveal an architectural culture in which tradition and innovation, continuity and change, are continuously negotiated—inviting a reconsideration of architecture as a cultural practice of adaptation and renewal.

title: Does Your Building Work or Does It Just Photograph Well? What Neuroscience and Use Data Could Teach Architects
text:
Does Your Building Work or Does It Just Photograph Well? What Neuroscience and Use Data Could Teach Architects

Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

title: Grand Terminal Doha / Hassell
text:
Grand Terminal Doha / Hassell

The Grand Terminal provides berths for two megaships, which can enjoy a variety of leisure and cultural amenities offered by the impressive waterside complex. Hassell Principal and Head of Design Ashley Munday said, "We are really excited that our Grand Terminal is beginning its life as a festival venue for the World Cup, but what excites us even more is its future as a loved piece of the city, embedded in the cultural fabric of Doha. It is a building that doesn't just have a singular function as a cruise terminal, but has been designed to absorb other uses during the year, like markets, exhibitions, and festivals. For us, this is a civic project that has to respond to many complex needs and requirements at once, but still has an 'outward' role to face the world and welcome people into a place that is really just emerging as a destination."

title: Four Projects in Thailand and Indonesia Recognized at the Steel Architectural Awards ASEAN 2026
text:
Four Projects in Thailand and Indonesia Recognized at the Steel Architectural Awards ASEAN 2026

An innovation campus, a corporate headquarters, a family home, and a community development in a remote peatland environment are the four winners of the Steel Architectural Awards ASEAN 2026. Located in Thailand and Indonesia, the projects explore how coated steel can respond to different climates, construction conditions, and patterns of use. The winners were announced at the ASEAN Awards Ceremony in Bangkok, Thailand, on November 20, 2026. They were selected from 12 finalists representing Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, following awards programs in each country.

title: COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities
text:
COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities

The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

title: Private House in Kaklebi  / Werkraum Design Architecture
text:
Private House in Kaklebi / Werkraum Design Architecture

The private house in Kaklebi, near Tbilisi, is composed of a series of timber-clad volumes rather than a single block, arranged to follow the slope of a wooded site and to preserve its existing mature trees. Distributed across multiple levels, the building reduces its own visual presence in the landscape while giving each level a distinct relationship to the terrain below.

title: The Portuguese Pavilion to Invite Four African Countries Through "Hands on the Ground" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
text:
The Portuguese Pavilion to Invite Four African Countries Through "Hands on the Ground" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

The Portuguese Directorate-General for the Arts announced on November 16 the curatorial proposal that will represent the country at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia in 2027. The selected project was "Mãos ao Chão (Hands on the Ground)," an artistic and curatorial proposal by Joanna Alice Helm, Remígio van Eys Chilaule and Samuel de Brito Gonçalves. It was chosen from a limited competition among three teams. The other two proposals were "Analog Twins" by Alice Clanet-Hallard, Edgar Brito, Francisco Lobo and Romea Mury, and "Matéria Viva — Os materiais da construção portuguesa e o saber que resiste" by Helena Botelho. The evaluation committee was composed of Álvaro Domingues, Andreia Garcia, João Gomes da Silva, Mariana Pestana and Tânia Teixeira.

Whether in Lisbon's medieval alleyways, along Haussmann's boulevards in Paris, on the wide avenues of car-oriented Chicago, or amid the metropolitan intensity of Avenida Paulista in São Paulo, different urban morphologies seem to give way to the same scene: crowds taking to the streets.

title: FORESTSCOPE / Sakakura Associates Architects and Engineers
text:
FORESTSCOPE / Sakakura Associates Architects and Engineers

A small spatial device that draws in and reflects the presence of the forest. Rather than simply looking out at the surrounding landscape, it directly brings in the image of the forest as it changes over time. After sunset, with projected images, it becomes a viewing hut that opens onto the outside world.

title: Abishkar Residence / SYSTEM architects - EKNC
text:
Abishkar Residence / SYSTEM architects - EKNC

ABISHKAR began not with the idea of a house, but with an attempt to understand the people who would inhabit it. At SYSTEM architects, design is approached as a participatory process. For this multi-generational home, planned for the parents and the families of their three sons, we began with a questionnaire about everyday life: how each person perceives space, what they value or avoid, their preferences, their need for privacy, and the kinds of spaces to which they feel naturally connected.

title: Sans Raison Renovation / Mountain Soil Interior Design
text:
Sans Raison Renovation / Mountain Soil Interior Design

Sans Raison is a 406-square-meter renovation project located in Jiading District, Shanghai. Originally an industrial building, the site retains much of its existing structure and the traces of its previous use. Rather than introducing an entirely new spatial arrangement, the design takes these existing conditions as a starting point, exploring how the building can accommodate new functions while retaining its original character.

title: Paper Stilt House / Esteban Uribe Architect
text:
Paper Stilt House / Esteban Uribe Architect

The Palafito de Papel is born from what already existed. It does not seek to be something new, but rather to belong, as if it had always existed in one of the most characteristic neighborhoods in the world: the stilt-house neighborhood of Castro, Chiloé. Wood and only wood. First, part of the existing structure was dismantled, as it was in a clear state of deterioration from decades of use and subsequent abandonment.

title: Futures thinking as an everyday design practice
text:
Futures thinking as an everyday design practice

Revisiting Three Horizons and exploring how we organize for what’s next

Throughout my career, I’ve used design practices to help organizations navigate change and deliver new capabilities and experiences. As a UX community, we’ve developed methods for understanding people’s needs, improving usability, engaging audiences, connecting complex systems, and making better decisions about what new features to build.

But as AI reshapes how we design, engineer, and deliver experiences, I believe the ability to think systematically and collectively about the future deserves a more central place in our organizations.

Speculative design, future-state service design, strategic foresight, trends research, and related practices give us ways to explore uncertainty and develop shared perspectives on where to go next. Yet in many organizations, this work is reserved for innovation workshops, vision sprints, or long-range strategy exercises.

What happens when the pace of technological change makes those occasional exercises insufficient?

When the assumptions underlying our tools, user behavior, professional roles, and ways of working can change within months rather than years, understanding emerging futures becomes more than a strategic planning activity.

As AI accelerates change, developing our collective ability to explore possible futures and shape emerging operating models may be one of the most important responsibilities of design leadership - and an essential part of the everyday decisions we make about the systems we design.

Revisiting the Three Horizons framework

One framework that has helped me think about how to put this into practice is Three Horizons. Originally developed by McKinsey as a corporate growth model, it was adapted by Anthony Hodgson, Bill Sharpe, and collaborators into a systems-thinking approach to understanding transformational change.

https://medium.com/media/2af5cbeb2c3445d49a0641c4a953bcf3/href

At Red Hat, our digital teams have adapted the Three Horizons view as a lens for aligning leadership perspectives and informing digital platform strategy, long before LLMs and agentic AI became central to the conversation.

What makes Three Horizons valuable is the way it helps teams understand the different systems and possibilities already competing for attention and resourcing in the present.

  • Horizon 1 (H1) represents the established system of technologies, practices, structures, and relationships through which we create value today.
  • Horizon 2 (H2) represents the new approaches emerging to address the limitations of existing capabilities, some extending the current system and others enabling a different future.
  • Horizon 3 (H3) represents a future system, where new patterns and possibilities may eventually become a fundamentally different standard of creating value.

A common misunderstanding is to treat these as sequential planning periods, when in reality all three horizons are present today. Consider how an enterprise digital organization might approach AI:

In H1, we’re maintaining and improving the established platforms, design and delivery processes, and customer experiences. Reliability, accessibility, and performance remain essential.

In H2, we’re introducing new intelligent systems into that environment. AI can accelerate content production, automate repetitive tasks, assist with coding, and help teams work more effectively across current pipelines.

In H3, we’re considering whether the underlying UX and digital platform model might change altogether. What happens when customer experiences are increasingly mediated by agents? When do intelligent systems reason about intent and coordinate system improvements across organizational boundaries?

What I appreciate about the framework is the space it creates for people who see change differently. Someone focused on H1 may be delivering updates to a system that thousands of customers depend on daily. Someone exploring H2 may be identifying opportunities to improve practices that no longer serve people well. And someone imagining H3 may be recognizing possibilities the organization isn’t yet prepared to pursue. Each perspective has something important to contribute.

A Three Horizons view isn’t just about imagining a different future, the value is in helping team members with different responsibilities develop a shared understanding of the present and make more informed choices about which horizons they are supporting.

Developing future consciousness

In October 2026, Bill Sharpe contributed a new chapter to the open-access collection The Three Horizons Approach, exploring how the framework “supports a process of participative repatterning between H1 and H3 in service of change, renewal, and transformation.”

We frequently ask design leaders to have a vision for the future. We expect them to anticipate change, identify opportunities, and guide their organization toward a desirable destination. But how do people develop that capability?

Sharpe’s work suggests a future consciousness can be strengthened through intentional practice. That matters because it moves futures thinking from something we associate with visionary individuals toward something organizations can learn together. He describes it as:

“An awareness of the future potential of the present moment.”

Rather than treating the future as a distant destination to predict, this invites us to recognize possibilities emerging through the activities, relationships, and choices of the present.

It also connects naturally to human-centered design. Design has long encouraged us to research people’s experiences, understand connections, explore alternatives, and learn through experimentation. These practices help us make sense of the present. They can also help us recognize emerging futures.

We don’t necessarily need to invent an entirely new discipline to bring futures thinking into our everyday work. But we do need to extend our attention beyond improving what exists toward asking what may be changing the systems we operate within.

Signals from a changing design and technology landscape

Throughout 2026, several perspectives from design and technology leaders have challenged my assumptions about how digital experiences and software will be created.

In October 2026, John Maeda delivered a lecture at Imperial College London titled Design and Engineering Are the Same Job Now.

His argument reflects an increasingly visible shift in the boundaries between disciplines. As generative systems become capable of producing both designs and working software, tasks once separated by specialized skills and production processes begin to overlap.

https://medium.com/media/ecea15679e972ce819bead37a75fdc7b/href

But the changes extend beyond how we create experiences. As AI increasingly participates in delivering those experiences, it’s also changing the relationship between people and the systems they use.

Maeda’s Design in Tech Report 2026: From UX to AX, explores this related transition from user experience toward agentic experience. As intelligent systems begin acting on people’s behalf, designers must consider not only how people accomplish tasks, but how they understand, evaluate, trust and control the actions those systems undertake.

This connects to my earlier exploration of moving from journey maps to control maps. When a system can independently take action, the design challenge extends beyond delivering pre-determined user interactions. People need to understand how responsibility, agency, and control are distributed between humans and machines. The value of a designer’s contribution doesn’t disappear, but the balance shifts from implementation tasks toward framing problems, technology and business alignment, evaluating results, and exercising judgment about what should be built.

This shift is also becoming visible in the practice of software engineering itself. Andrej Karpathy has been exploring this parallel transformation. In his October 2026 HackerTube experiment, he demonstrated how an AI coding agent could build and deploy a YouTube-style discovery application built around videos recommended on Hacker News in approximately two hours, with little conventional hands-on programming.

Taking that a step further, Amp, a small team building an AI coding agent for software development, published their October 2026 podcast episode titled The Company of the Future. The team described how their 21-person startup operates without conventional departments, quarterly objectives, or mandatory code review. Their approach challenges familiar assumptions about how software teams should be structured, suggesting that agentic capabilities may enable fundamentally different ways of organizing and delivering work.

https://medium.com/media/768dfb0ab3ca3511a60d251b7f323ee5/href

Earlier in July 2026, the same team published a provocative episode, The Local Dev Env is Dead, exploring a development model where agents operate in parallel across isolated, remotely controlled environments while engineers focus increasingly on defining product objectives and evaluating outcomes.

While Amp’s practices may not translate directly to larger enterprises, they offer an interesting glimpse of how emerging technologies could reshape the systems and structures we’ve built around product and experience delivery. They also raise questions about which other assumptions about how we design, engineer, and organize work might become unnecessary.

The developments from frontier AI labs and enterprise technology providers add another dimension. At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, advances in Codex and agent infrastructure emphasized delegating substantial work to systems operating beyond an individual developer’s laptop. At Google’s Gemini at Work 2026, the keynote introduced a more unified agent model spanning knowledge work, applications, data, and software development. Anthropic’s November 2026 introduction of Claude Ship extends agent participation into reviewing code changes, addressing problems, and applying team-defined approval policies. And IBM’s watsonx Orchestrate developments, presented at TechXchange 2026, emphasize the need to discover, secure, evaluate, and govern agents across complex enterprise environments.

Each development provides a perspective on how our existing systems might evolve with AI. What interests me is how these agentic capabilities will influence future organizational structures. New forms of agent coordination may change the importance of particular design and development workflows, and require entirely different approaches to how teams are organized.

The organizational patterns beneath the technology

Another idea from Sharpe’s October 2026 Three Horizons update offers a useful way to connect these possibilities: pattern = participation.

Organizations persist through the relationships and activities of the people participating in them. Operating models are continually reproduced through decisions, responsibilities, specialized skills, approvals, incentives, and expectations about how work should happen.

When people, and increasingly AI agents, begin participating differently, the patterns of an organization may begin to change as well. AI agents are not participants in the same human sense, but their growing involvement in executing work, coordinating activities, and informing decisions introduces new relationships and responsibilities into established systems.

Consider a large enterprise digital organization. Introducing AI assistance into existing production workflows may improve efficiency while preserving the underlying operating model. Teams continue to work across the same applications, handoffs, and responsibilities, even as individual tasks become faster and more automated.

But what happens when agents begin coordinating work across those boundaries? The change may extend beyond the tools people use to the relationships through which work gets done.

This distinction connects to an important feature of Three Horizons. Within H2, some innovations reinforce and extend the established system, while others begin creating the conditions for an H3 successor. These are described as H2− and H2+ innovations, respectively.

Neither approach is inherently right or wrong. Maintaining established systems remains essential, particularly where organizations have ongoing responsibilities to customers and employees. At the same time, exploring new capabilities can reveal opportunities to rethink relationships and constraints that have shaped how organizations operate for years.

For design and technology leadership, this is an interesting dimension of futures thinking. Rather than examining only which workflows might be automated, we can begin to consider which relationships might change, which capabilities remain valuable, and what new patterns of work could become possible. Understanding our existing portfolio, tech stack, workflows, skills, dependencies, and operating practices helps us recognize the patterns we’re participating in today. Some relationships remain necessary. Others reflect constraints that emerging technologies may remove.

The opportunity isn’t simply to introduce AI into the work we’re already doing. It’s to become more curious about the different ways people, intelligent systems, and organizations might work together in the future.

Experimenting with new relationships

Sharpe introduces another concept that I find particularly useful for translating futures thinking into practice: the minimum viable pattern. Rather than focusing solely on a product or technical capability, he draws our attention to the relationships and commitments through which a different system might begin to emerge.

“Entrepreneurs often talk of their minimum viable product, meaning the simplest version that can be released that will get the business going. I have found that borrowing this notion and converting it to a minimum viable pattern is a powerful way to connect people to thinking about the relationships from which the third horizon can grow.”
— Bill Sharpe, Deepening the Patterning of Hope in Three Horizons (2026)

What interests me about this concept is the shift in what we choose to experiment with. Design teams are familiar with prototyping products, services, and experiences. But as AI begins changing how work is coordinated, we also have opportunities to experiment with the roles and responsibilities that make different operating models possible.

This isn’t entirely new territory for design. Service design and DesignOps have long helped us understand the people, processes, dependencies, and organizational systems behind the experiences we create.

https://medium.com/media/f7769b313037e53291d3765b60bb6b4a/href
“The visualization of relationships in [service] blueprints uncovers potential improvements and ways to eliminate redundancy.”
— Sarah Gibbons, Service Blueprints: Definition, Nielsen Norman Group (2017).

What’s changing is the opportunity to extend these practices beyond improving established workflows toward exploring new ways for humans and intelligent agents to collaborate.

In AI in Service Design: A New Framework for Hybrid Human–AI Service Encounters, Marzia Mortati and Giovanna Viana Mundstock Freitas examine how service design changes when both humans and AI can participate as service providers or users. Their research considers interactions extending beyond traditional human-facing experiences, including services accessed by AI on people’s behalf and interactions occurring directly between intelligent systems.

This expands what designers may need to make visible, understand, and evaluate. A service blueprint might increasingly account for agents making decisions across systems, or interacting with services without a conventional human interface.

Rather than simply mapping handoffs, approvals, and responsibilities, we can begin experimenting with how people and intelligent agents share context, coordinate activities, make decisions, and maintain accountability.

A conventional content automation experiment might evaluate how effectively an agent can complete an established task. A minimum viable pattern experiment could instead bring design, engineering, content, and operations together to explore how a different combination of people, agents, and services might deliver the intended outcome.

The experiment becomes a way to learn about emerging organizational relationships, not simply validate technical performance. It may reveal a promising alternative or help us understand why certain responsibilities and practices remain necessary.

For design leadership, I see an opportunity to bring our methods of inquiry, prototyping, service design, and experimentation into the design of work itself. Not to claim ownership of organizational operations, but to help multidisciplinary teams explore how new capabilities might change the systems and relationships through which they create value.

Developing human capability alongside technology

Exploring new operating models also raises an important question about the people who will work within them. As AI changes the boundaries of our disciplines and the activities we perform, how do we help people develop the capabilities to participate in what comes next?

In 2019, Don Norman and Karel Vredenburg founded the Future of Design Education initiative to reconsider how designers should be prepared for increasingly complex challenges. Norman outlined the effort in his essay, The Future of Design Education, questioning how design education could better prepare people to work across disciplines and address complex sociotechnical systems.

The effort culminated in a 2023 special issue of She Ji: The Journal of Design, Economics, and Innovation, edited by Meredith Davis. In the opening article, Rethinking Design Education, Davis and Hugh Dubberly examine how design practice is expanding beyond the production of individual artifacts toward the stewardship of interconnected products, services, and systems. They also consider how design’s responsibilities increasingly extend into organizational strategy, governance, and the longer-term consequences of decisions.

A related contribution by Hugh Dubberly and Paul Pangaro, How Might We Help Designers Understand Systems?, develops this thinking further. Their work explores how designers can learn to recognize system boundaries, relationships, feedback, and patterns of behavior, using shared models to make complex systems more understandable. What I find relevant is the emphasis on developing a common language for working across disciplines, rather than treating systems understanding as a specialized area of expertise.

Although these papers focus on design education, their implications extend naturally to practicing professionals and organizational leaders. Most of us spend far more of our careers learning within organizations than preparing for them through formal education. And as AI changes how experiences are created and work is coordinated, the need to understand the systems surrounding our individual responsibilities becomes increasingly important.

The initiative predates the recent acceleration in generative AI, but its questions are remarkably timely. As design and engineering become more closely connected, what should people understand about each other’s disciplines? As agents take on more sophisticated responsibilities, how do we develop the judgment to evaluate their actions and consequences? And how do we ensure that greater technological capability also expands people’s opportunities to learn and contribute?

In his August 2026 essay, My Verdict on AI: Positives, Negatives, & Hope, Vredenburg explores Symbiotic Design Thinking, an approach emphasizing active human participation in AI-assisted work rather than immediately delegating the thinking itself. Scott Belsky, former Chief Product Officer of Adobe and author of The Messy Middle, raises complementary questions in his September and October Implications essays, considering how intelligent agents may change user experience, the value of authentic human contributions, and what we risk losing as we outsource more of our reasoning and creative exploration.

https://medium.com/media/a2b78f319a7ead20b1a6ef3e5dae4c7d/href

These perspectives invite us to look beyond productivity as the primary measure of AI’s value. The opportunity isn’t simply to help people accomplish more with intelligent systems, but to explore how those systems might support deeper understanding, better judgment, and new forms of collaboration. As implementation becomes easier, the ability to ask meaningful questions, evaluate alternatives, and understand the consequences for human agency may become even more valuable.

Expanding the design practice for the AI era

The future isn’t simply something we prepare for. It’s something we learn to understand and influence together, through the choices we make and the work we do every day.

Looking across the AI developments in 2026, I’m struck by how much of the change we’re experiencing extends beyond technology itself. The boundaries between disciplines are becoming more fluid, established operating models are being reconsidered, and intelligent systems are introducing new relationships between people, tools, and organizations. These shifts invite us to think more broadly about the systems we design, the capabilities we develop, and the futures our decisions may help shape.

This is where design leadership has an opportunity to contribute. Not by claiming a privileged understanding of the future, but by helping create the conditions in which collective inquiry becomes part of how organizations operate.

These aren’t entirely new responsibilities for design. Research and trend analysis can help us recognize emerging behaviors alongside present needs. Systems mapping can reveal the assumptions and dependencies underlying familiar experiences. Speculative design and prototyping can make alternative futures tangible, while experimentation helps us investigate which new relationships and capabilities may be practical.

Futures thinking doesn’t need to remain a separate exercise in imagining tomorrow. It can become part of how we understand, question, and shape the systems we’re designing today.

References:

Kaplan, K. (2019). DesignOps 101. Nielsen Norman Group.

title: Four hidden dimensions of effective teams
text:
Four hidden dimensions of effective teams

Company success isn’t about following a magic formula or hacking the corporate game; it’s about using the context and information around us with purpose.

This year, I had the honor of joining a revolutionary LATAM design convention in Lima, Perú, where I was invited to speak about design and team strategy, two topics I’m most passionate about.

Months before the convention, I reflected on how to send a strong message that sparks questions and encourages the audience to take action to increase design’s influence in corporate decision-making, something we (the designers) have long believed we deserve by right.

One topic I highlighted during the talk was an artifact I developed early this year that helped me bridge design and company strategy and brought me closer to strategic conversations, with promising results so far.

Building this simple new tool helped me validate a long-standing personal belief: stop accepting that designers only generate value through “cosmetics,” since some people still think design is just the visual layer of functionality.

The common language in all companies.

One idea that resonated strongly with the audience was the fact that everything we do as designers has a monetary consequence (it shouldn’t be a novelty nowadays), no matter the size of the solution, idea, or context; so thinking in numbers is one thing that should be embraced from junior design positions. Numbers aren’t just money from users; they’re everything that produces it. In that sense, developing the self-awareness to understand and measure our own work towards results could put us in a strategic position within a company.

How to measure effectiveness? The four dimensions you overlook.

This isn’t just about having KPIs or OKRs in a team; it’s about understanding all measurable resources that show how effective we are as a company.

I’ve identified some basic dimensions that define an entire company’s dynamics and, with them, all the possible challenges within. Although these dimensions seem obvious in every company, after 20+ years in the tech industry, the truth is they aren’t, and we still struggle, over and over, with the same old issues.

How did this perspective come about? Well, it wasn’t really a discovery, but rather connecting disparate dots—things people overlooked when executing projects or having conversations.

I ask my teammates a few basic questions that can paint a picture of a company or team’s state. I used to ask these questions informally, but I didn’t always have a complete picture of the overall situation. That is why, after some time, I decided to organize a set of measurable dimensions that could clearly diagnose my environment and its main challenges.

The sum of all dimensions is a metric that reflects the maturity and effectiveness level of a company or its teams, helping build a solid foundation for product creation and making the process more rewarding.

Use this metric to acknowledge the state of the company and start having relevant conversations:

The Structure

The first dimension refers to how people, teams, or areas are connected; it comes first because it reveals the system we are working in, including both positive and negative factors.

The structure dimension is built from inner concepts that, together, give us a full picture of how the system of connection works. Why is this dimension important? Because it delimits the field of action and its actors.

1. Role definition
This is the first aspect I ask when I want to understand the state of a team; it is surprisingly common to encounter companies and teams that lack information regarding this fundamental concept. For some reason, some people consider it normal to hire someone with no plan for the company or the professional.

The lack of information about a role reveals the company’s level of corporate maturity. At this point, we can find several reasons regarding this issue: “We are in a digital transformation, so we’re figuring out the design roles,” “We brought you here (the leader) to help us build the team vision,” “This team originally was under the CMO or CTO management, and his/her knowledge was limited in terms of user experience,” “We are a startup, we wear a lot of hats, so you build your own role.”

Some of those reasons may be valid, but my critique around this is a simple question: how do you move for years (sometimes under a lot of stress) without knowing your boundaries or responsibilities? I’ve seen a lot of designers immersed in constant uncertainty because they don’t know their range of actions, all disguised under the condescending phrase: “I do what I’m asked.”

I think not having a role makes you vulnerable to whatever circumstances arise, which, in my opinion, is highly detrimental to professional growth because your job keeps changing.

A clear understanding of product roles lays the foundation for how effective teams operate within a system.

2. Career path
Moving forward, the career path is the next level of structure maturity in teams or companies. Part of my assessment when joining a team is understanding all possible growth tracks within the Structure I’ll lead. When a career path is missing, the negative effects might be several.

In the short term, the impact might not be as visible, so people could feel “comfortable” for a couple of years, but the thing with this issue is that time is inevitable; eventually, when years have passed, people will realize they are way behind the latest skills in the market, which will create great frustration and a sense of wasting valuable time doing the same job without increasing their talents.

3. Org chart
Knowing who to report to, who to lead, or who to work with as a peer matters. Part of being effective is knowing who to talk to to drive results. Org charts are often dead, outdated documentation; people only see them the first week of a new job. Over time, I’ve realized this artifact is fundamental for decision-making or showing results. From a design perspective, org charts can also be stakeholder maps or the canvas for making strategic decisions for the team.

If org charts aren’t visible in a production dynamic, effective communication is almost impossible, and the consequences will hit sooner or later. That said, here’s the latest concept for the structure dimension.

4. Working flows
Imagine you have a clear understanding of your team’s structure, but communication isn’t always effective. Why? Well, it is because we haven’t connected the roles into a functional dynamic, and without that, we have nothing; imagine a classical orchestra without a director; it’s quite a mess.

Designers are experts at figuring out user flows to connect a product with clients, but they don’t think to do the same exercise to connect roles on a team to other teams towards a product goal. Strong working flows make product decisions more effective, and time will be your ally.

Performance

It is obvious we need to talk about performance as the second effective dimension, but far from having KPIs, this approach is different; it is about how much we know about success for the company and us. As for the structure, the performance dimension has inner concepts that feed into the overall dimension, and I’ll guide you through each one.

1. Company goal
I’ve been part of projects where this information is nonexistent, or teams aren’t aware of it and make decisions with a biased vision; the result? Narrowed approaches, sometimes disconnected from the main company strategic plan; sooner or later, the consequences of working away from what the company is pursuing can be expensive.

We used to think the company’s goal was something shared in an all-hands meeting, and then nobody remembered it. Still, keeping this goal present in every project helps us filter hard decisions and create more accurate, business-driven developments. Bring these goals to the next project pitch, and stakeholders will embrace your idea more than if you pitch something amazing but far from a business priority.

2. Area and team goals
Digging deep into goals, the next level is the area goals. This information is more visible than company goals. They are closer to us since we operate in a more tactical field, but remember that area goals should build toward the company objective, so being aware of the previous concept matters.

Are you aware of this information when executing something? I would say most teammates will say, “I’m not sure,” so don’t assume they are clueless about this.

Why do I bother to highlight this concept? The answer lies in how other members of the company still perceive our work: as something merely aesthetic, rather than an effort toward effectiveness and conversion. I’d wager that if designers approached a board of directors with a strategy focused on business objectives, the results would be different.

3. Installed capacity
I’ve said it before, and I’ll keep pointing out this issue: are we reactive, or do we have the capacity to react? Hard pill to swallow, right? It is sad to see how design leaders just follow in a huge reactive storm, where the day-to-day is about surviving others’ mess.

Not knowing your team’s capacity or your teammates’ capacity compels you to follow orders without negotiation, which is, most of the time, negative in every way.

As a leader, discussing capacity reveals more about you than you think; it gives you power and control over the project’s time and decisions. On the contrary, not knowing this information, as I said before, makes you accept others’ conditions with no chance to state your point of view.

4. Definition of success/failure
How do you know your team is doing right? Or wrong? Are you one of those who go with the flow? Some days we’re good, and some days everything stinks. This concept has nothing to do with accomplishing OKRs; it’s about having clear team boundaries: what to celebrate and what to penalize.

This concept should be repeatedly visible on every team, and it should become the DNA for how we operate and behave in front of others.

Building a healthy DNA for the team will create a reputation for you and your team, something that can be well rewarded in company strategic moments.

Time

The third dimension is about knowing the time we expend doing something. As you may know, time is money, and not being aware of it can lead us to an ineffective spiral with negative consequences.

One way to figure out how ineffective teams are in terms of time is simple: in ongoing projects, there is often no awareness of stages or changes that come in at the wrong time and slow down the team’s output. In these scenarios, a medium initiative can become large, expensive, and frustrating for teams.

The concepts that build the time dimensions are related to hours and their usage:

1. Team execution hours
This concept is about tracking how much time the team spends on projects; this information is usually overlooked in strategic conversations, and without it, we can’t measure how fast the team is or how long projects take.

Tracking team effort over time will give us a better perspective on how to respond to future challenges, so that the next time we face a project, we’ll be ready to provide a better time estimate.

In planning sessions with the team, having a project time matrix will give the team a solid starting point instead of jumping into the unknown without a clue how long this challenge will last.

2. Strategy hours
The other side of time is what we spend on conversations, planning, or solving situations for the team. In senior design positions, this time is crucial to account for; we will not always be able to execute tasks if our job demands that we oversee multiple teams or duties.

I recommend having some sort of artifact that can back you up when showing results to execs; whether execution or strategic time, it is important to be aware of the amount of time (money) you represent for the company.

Money

Since time is money, other monetary situations shouldn’t be strange for us. Not knowing anything about money (the common language in companies) will relegate us to a merely executing position. At the same time, other profiles will discuss whether it is profitable to take on a project.

We don’t need to be financial experts to understand our resource costs, and that’s enough. Some of the basic notions of money issues to control are:

1. Team and role cost
How much does your team cost? It is a question that is not always on our radar. Still, once you realize you have a team cost of X, you can approach project planning from a different perspective, especially when comparing it with budgets.

If you apply this information to your planning conversations, you can make smarter moves in hiring people or shifting resources across multiple initiatives.

2. Projects budget
In some decision tables, every conversation, context, or challenge starts with the budget, so you should understand the project’s financial scope from the beginning.

This information may not be attractive to junior design positions, but for leaders, it is crucial to manage and understand.

Money and time are rare areas of knowledge among designers, so developing them will put us on a different level when approaching projects or hard conversations in companies.

My takeaway from this:

There are several aptitudes we can adopt to thrive in companies, whether big or small; the goal is still the same: converting money. Around success in companies, there is way too much information from modern history to read and watch. Still, in design environments, which I think is fascinating, I feel like there is little information on how to use our expertise to our advantage in a strategic way; maybe I’m wrong, but if we’re still struggling to show our value in companies, it’s because we haven’t figured out how to back up our discipline, right?

I believe the basics always work best, and the four dimensions of effective teams come from watching teams over 20 years of experience in different contexts and industries. Maybe this is not the holy formula for success, but at least it gives us a different perspective on how to use the information that is always there, but we don’t see or use, and let other people make decisions for us.

To write this article, I want to credit all the fantastic information sources and other authors who have written about related topics, each from an exciting, different perspective.

title: Who draws the in-betweens?
text:
Who draws the in-betweens?

Every line we draw around AI measures the tool. Authorship has always lived in the decisions.

Earlier this month Dior released Christian Dior’s Night in Color, a holiday short directed by Sylvain Chomet, the animator behind The Triplets of Belleville and The Illusionist. A week after release, the internet had already reached its verdict. People had paused, zoomed in, counted the fingers, and decided it was AI.

https://medium.com/media/b0e597b691aae940498b481aa00feecb/href

Chomet and his producer, Aton Soumache, answered in an interview with Variety. Artists drew the characters, they say, the backgrounds and the key poses, and around twenty people worked on the film for seven months. Then came the detail that set everyone off. The team had used automated interpolation, software that generates the frames between keyframes, for what Soumache called “a very small part of the process.” Chomet said it automated the repetitive, mechanical side of animation and left the creative side alone.

A lot of people read that as a confession, but for me it was something else. Until then, I’d mostly thought about AI the way people in my job usually do: as a question of tools, speed and budgets. This was the first time I looked at it through an artist’s eyes. I tried to imagine Chomet reading the accusations, a man who has spent his whole career drawing by hand, being told his film wasn’t his. And I think I understood what must have gone through his head in that moment: what is the difference?

His films have always had in-betweeners. Other people always drew part of his films, following his keys, his timing, his idea of how things should move. So if he drew the keys and a machine filled in some of the frames between them, is the film still his? And if it isn’t, where exactly did it stop being his?

I want to try answering that honestly, by following the lines people usually draw and seeing whether they hold.

The first line: a human hand on every frame

The instinctive answer is that art means a person drew it. But that has never been true of animation, which is why the Dior case is so useful.

For most of its history, hand-drawn animation has worked like this: A lead animator draws the key poses, the drawings that carry the action and the acting. Assistants and in-betweeners fill in the frames between them, sometimes dozens for every second of film. Their names sit far down the credits, when they appear at all, and I’ve never heard anyone leave a cinema praising an in-between. The lead animator’s job is to direct. They decide how every movement should feel, look at every pass, push back on whatever doesn’t work, and keep going until the whole film looks like it came from a single hand.

So the “human hand on every frame” line was already crossed decades ago, by other humans nobody credited. Swapping some of those humans for software leaves the lead animator doing exactly the same job. The keys are still theirs and so is every decision about what stays and what gets redrawn. What changes is speed and cost, and I don’t see how speed makes a drawing less yours. Anyone who animated in Flash in the 2000s used tweens, automated in-betweening under another name, and nobody called it the end of the craft.

To be fair to the critics, some frames really were ugly, and some of the flaws looked a lot like what people have learned to recognize as AI artifacts. Maybe the interpolation produced them, maybe not. But these things on their own prove very little. Chomet explained that extra fingers appear when you’re selling fast movement, and any animator will tell you the same. Smears and multiples are an old trick. If counting fingers were the test, half of classic cartoons from the 1930s would be guilty.

Hand-drawn in-betweens have always had their bad frames too. Pause almost any classic cartoon and you’ll find a face that collapses for a frame or a hand that melts into the next pose. Somebody drew those, worked against a deadline, and nobody checked closely enough. We forgive them because we watch the film, not individual frames. Imperfections in a production people love read as charm, or as the cost of making something. The same imperfections in a production people already suspect read as evidence.

The second line: the machine has to be under control

The more elaborate version of the objection goes like this: Fine, tools have always done part of the work, but those tools were predictable. A generative model isn’t, so using it means accepting whatever comes out.

Animation has a good test case for this: hair and fur. Ever since Sulley’s coat in Monsters, Inc., a whole genre of films has existed partly to show off how good fur simulation had become. Nobody draws those hairs: artists define the groom, density, length and how it moves, and a simulation computes millions of strands frame by frame. The result is about as machine-made as an image gets, but we call it craft, because the artist decided what the fur should be and the software carried it out.

I don’t think generative tools are as far from that as people assume. When I describe a shot to one of the video tools I use, say a rooftop at dusk with a slow push-in on a woman looking at the city, I don’t get a random picture, I get something close to what I described, similar to the way a camera operator brings back something close to your brief. Then the real work starts, because these tools now sit inside an ordinary editor. I can retime the push-in, cut the shot shorter, regrade the sky, rework the sound, and each of those changes does exactly what I tell it to.

Photographers have lived with this forever: on the street you don’t control the light, the passers-by or the clouds, but you choose the moment, the frame and the edit. Nobody says the photo isn’t yours because you didn’t place the pedestrians. Nobody controls everything, not photographers, not animators, not anyone. What matters is whether you shaped the result, and AI doesn’t change that.

The third line: real work takes effort

This is the one I feel most personally, because it’s usually framed as being “on the side” of people like me.

Some of the websites I design are the projects I live for, complex and animated and thought through down to the scroll, and those take weeks because the effort is the point. But creative work has always been tied to commissions and invoices, and next to those projects there’s a steady stream of small sites for businesses that can’t spend much or wait long. Anyone in my industry will tell you that most of the website market runs on templates. Someone buys a theme, changes the colors, fonts, copy and photos, and ships it. Nobody calls that a betrayal of craft. It’s a service sized to a budget.

The same goes for the pieces inside a site. A signup flow or a checkout is a solved problem, built on patterns users expect to behave the same everywhere, and a “creative” checkout is usually a worse one. I’ve never built one from scratch for its own sake, I use a proven component, one made and shared precisely so people like me don’t have to reinvent it, and configure it to fit. If I generate that same standard pattern instead of cloning it, I genuinely can’t see what I’ve stolen, or from whom.

Templates aren’t only a way to do less, either. Used well, they’re a floor. If the checkout, the navigation and the basic layout are already solved, the hours I’d have spent rebuilding them go into the parts nobody has seen before: the interaction that takes three days to tune, the animation that makes a site feel like the brand it belongs to. Generated components work the same way. Starting from something solid leaves more time and energy for going past it.

We’ve also watched this happen before. When Webflow, Squarespace and WordPress spread, designers said they would kill the profession and make every site look alike. They were partly right about the second part: the cheap end of the market filled up with lookalikes. But something else happened that nobody predicted: a whole generation of designers came in through those tools. People who never learned to code, who would never have been hired by an agency, started building sites on their own, and some of them turned out to be very good. No-code didn’t lower the ceiling. It raised it, because more people with taste could finally reach it.

Some work needs artistic value and effort, some just needs to exist and work. The same tools served both, and insisting on effort everywhere mostly makes the small client pay for our self-image.

The fourth line: you need the skill

If effort isn’t the line, maybe skill is. You should at least be able to make the thing yourself.

Ira Glass has a well-known idea about this, often called “the taste gap”. People get into creative work because they have good taste, and for years their work falls short of it. The only way across that gap, he says, is to keep making work until your hands catch up. What I think generative tools do is close the gap from the other side. Say I can’t draw well, but I can sketch the character I want for my game. A tool helps me turn that sketch into a finished design, but it doesn’t get there on its own. I push it, version after version, deciding on the shoes, the hair, the eyes, the marks of its skin, until it looks exactly the way I imagined. The tool lent me its hands, but every decision was mine.

That deciding is the part that matters. As Nielsen Norman Group points out, these tools fill skill gaps, but being able to make something you couldn’t make before doesn’t mean it’s good.

I live a version of this every week: I’d love to promote my work on social media with proper videos, with long cuts, animations timed to what I’m saying, captions that land on the right word, a title card that’s actually mine. I know what good looks like, because I watch plenty of it. What I don’t have is the budget to hire an editor for every post, and the honest alternative to a generated starting point was never a commissioned video, but rather no video at all.

So I start from what the tools give me and work on it. Along the way I’m learning things I never had a reason to learn: what makes an intro hold people past the first seconds, how different montage styles change the pace, where a cut should fall so the point lands. Some editors will get less work because people like me can do this now, and I don’t pretend otherwise. But this particular job was never going to exist, because the money for it was never there. If anything, a self-made video that works is the kind of thing that eventually justifies hiring a professional for the bigger one.

The worry is that skipping the struggle stunts people, the way pocket calculators were supposed to ruin arithmetic. They didn’t. Kids still learn math, and the ones who love it still go deep. Glass’s advice to make a lot of work still holds; you just get more rounds of making, judging and fixing in a year. The constraints don’t vanish, they move up, from “can I draw this hand” to “do I have anything worth saying.”

Cheap making also means cheap failure, and that matters more than it sounds. If one of my videos flops, I’ve lost an afternoon, not a client budget, so I can afford to try the odd idea and see what happens. The same logic works at the top of the industry. Hollywood keeps making remakes because a film that costs two hundred million dollars has to be a safe bet. Lower the cost of making things and you lower the cost of taking a risk, which is usually where the original ideas come from.

The fifth line: it learned from other people’s work

The last line people draw is about where the tools came from. Models were trained on artists’ work without asking, and for a lot of people that settles it.

I’m aware this is an unpopular thing to say, but here’s my confession, if it is one: so was I. So was every artist who ever lived. Nothing we make comes from nowhere: it comes from everything I’ve seen, played, watched, read and lived through, other people’s work included, and nobody signed a release before any of it got into my head. The more varied that mix, the better the work tends to be. There’s even a name for it: the Medici Effect, from a 2004 book by Frans Johansson. It’s named after the Florentine banking family who, in the fifteenth century, funded sculptors, painters, architects, scientists, poets and philosophers and brought them together in the same city. Johansson’s argument is that the Renaissance came from that mixing, from ideas crossing between fields, more than from any single genius. Creativity mostly happens where influences meet.

Ghibli is a good example for this. Isao Takahata and Hayao Miyazaki both said a French animated film, Paul Grimault’s La Bergère et le Ramoneur, later reworked as Le Roi et l’Oiseau, shaped how they thought about animation. Miyazaki once said that watching it taught him how to use space vertically. Grimault never gave permission, and nobody would call Castle in the Sky a Grimault film. The influence went in, got mixed with everything else they loved, and came out as something that was theirs.

In March 2025 a new image model made “Ghibli style” the internet’s favorite filter, and for a few weeks it seemed everyone had turned their selfies, pets and memes into Miyazaki frames. Alongside them, an old clip came back: Miyazaki in 2016, watching a demo of AI-generated animation and calling it an insult to life itself. I respect that. He’s entitled to never want the technology anywhere near his work. But look at what the trend actually produced: millions of images that look like Ghibli, and not one of them is a Ghibli movie.

That’s the part I think people miss. Even if I could draw perfect Ghibli-style cartoons, that wouldn’t make me Ghibli, or an artist. Ghibli is Ghibli because of its stories, its characters, its worlds, and a style that bends from film to film to serve them. A model can absorb the style, but that was never what made those films great.

There is one real difference, and I don’t want to skip it. When I learn from Miyazaki, I become one more artist with some of his influence in me. A model learns from everyone at once and can produce that influence on demand, for anyone, at almost no cost. That changes the market for people who draw for a living, and it’s a fair thing to worry about. Lost dog — or lost designer? on UX Collective presses on the same point, asking where influence ends, authorship begins and appropriation becomes exploitation, and it’s right that human learning and AI training aren’t the same thing. But that difference is an argument about markets, not authorship. The question this essay is asking is who made the thing, and a style on its own has never answered it.

Where authorship actually lives

Put those lines side by side and they share something. Every one of them measures the tool: whose hand, how predictable, how much effort, how much skill, what it learned from. Authorship has always been somewhere else, in the decisions.

Designers have been circling this question since the first image generators. As Wait, who made this? notes, the questions about authorship, copyright and compensation raised by DALL-E and Midjourney still don’t have answers. Here’s the way of thinking about it that has helped me most.

Think of any piece of work as a grid of small decisions: the shape, the color, the timing, the cut. Some cells you fill in yourself. The rest get filled by whatever you’re working with. A template fills them with someone else’s design choices, an in-betweener with their own hand, a fur simulator with physics, a model with patterns from its training data. Nobody fills in every cell, and nobody ever has.

So instead of a line, I think there’s a matrix: the more of the grid you actually filled in yourself, the more of the work is yours. That explains why lazy AI art feels so empty, since almost none of its cells were decided by anyone. It also explains why Chomet’s film is Chomet’s, why my sketched character is mine, and why a template with the stock photos left in doesn’t really belong to anybody.

It also explains what the backlash keeps getting wrong. From the outside nobody can see the decisions. A viewer can’t tell a character refined over days from one typed in a single line, so “contains AI” becomes shorthand for “nobody cared,” and the finger-counting starts. Sometimes the shorthand is right. Often, as with Dior, it lands on people who drew most of the film by hand.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is an even clearer case. It was one of the most celebrated games of 2025, a debut from a studio that obviously poured itself into every frame, and it won Game of the Year at The Game Awards. Then it came out that the developer had used generative AI for a handful of placeholder textures, a few of which shipped by mistake and were patched out within days. The Indie Game Awards took back its Game of the Year and Debut Game prizes anyway. You can argue about the rules, but nobody who played that game could say nobody cared. And I don’t accept the framing that what we value is “knowing a human made it,” as if a machine in the pipeline erased the person. Every film of the last thirty years has had machines in the pipeline.

That puts some responsibility on us as creators. If people can’t see the process, we should show it. Dior’s campaign leaned on “traditional craftsmanship,” and Chomet said in Dior’s own promotional video that they work just like in the 1940s. Then an interview revealed software in the pipeline, and a good part of the anger came from finding out afterwards. Being open about how something was made costs nothing, and it’s the only way “they used AI” turns into a description instead of an accusation.

What this means for people like me

I’m not writing this from a safe distance. The small sites I build for clients on a budget are precisely the work these tools are learning to do, and I’d be lying if I said that doesn’t worry me. Some of that work will go away, and some of it is probably mine.

It’s sad. It’s also true, and the first doesn’t change the second. There’s no version of this where the tools get un-invented and the market goes back to how it was. Portrait painters, typesetters and the ink-and-paint artists who colored animation cels by hand all went through some version of this, and none of them got the old world back by refusing to look at the new one. There will be more sameness too: research on AI-assisted writing found it helps weaker writers most while making their stories more alike. Designers are already seeing the interface version of this. AI made everyone a creator, not a designer describes how generated products start to feel interchangeable, because the models lean toward statistically safe versions of “good UI.” Taste is not a feature starts from the same study to argue that AI makes taste more important, not less. Pretending none of this is happening won’t make it go away.

What I can do is be honest about which part of my job was ever really mine. It was never typing out the checkout. It was deciding what a site should feel like, what to leave out, what a client needs even when they ask for something else. The technical know-how is getting cheaper. Taste and a way of seeing aren’t, and that’s the part I intend to sell. I’m not the only designer making that bet: AI is coming for our design jobs, but it can’t touch taste argues that taste, not technical skill, is where a designer’s edge is moving.

The part that stays

Some say judgment will be automated next, and the machines will end up filling in every cell of the grid. I doubt it. Machines can already predict what moves an audience on average; that’s what recommendation feeds do. What they can’t know is what you want to say, and since creative work is self-expression, that part stays with you.

For a lot of people, the only things standing between them and what they wanted to make were money and technique, and those are getting easier to get past. What they make once they’re through is still up to them.

I know plenty of people won’t agree with this, including some whose work I really admire. If you’re one of them, I’d like to hear it. Maybe there’s a line I skipped, or one I stepped over too quickly. The comments are open: tell me where you’d draw the line. I’ll read everything, and I’m open to being convinced.

title: Yes, Party Jeans Are A Thing — And These $54 Ones Are Cool-Girl Approved
text:
Yes, Party Jeans Are A Thing — And These $54 Ones Are Cool-Girl Approved

Every December, I briefly become convinced that I need a sequin dress or sparkly pants. I picture myself wearing them to a party, conveniently forgetting how many parties I actually go to and how often I end up sitting cross-legged on somebody’s couch. True Whitaker has a better idea for that particular evening. Her dream outfit for a friend’s holiday soiree includes a cashmere sweater, vintage boots, and low-rise jeans.

She’s already road-tested a version of the look, albeit on a fake plane. In Old Navy’s ’90s-inspired Jingle Jet campaign, Whitaker wore the brand’s Low Rise Baggy Wide-Leg Jeans with a sweater. “Love a perfect silhouette,” Whitaker tells Refinery29. The dark indigo is what sells me on these for a party. The wash has enough depth to sit next to your fanciest going-out tops. And the fit has the kind of slouch that makes a good sweater feel a little less proper. I’d go with a cashmere crewneck that hits right around the waistband and a pointed-toe boot that peeks out from under the wide hem. If you already own both, the jeans are the only piece you need to shop.

Whitaker shares the Jingle Jet cabin with Alan Cumming, Paris Hilton, Charli D’Amelio, Meg Stalter, Vidya Gopalan and her family, and Magic the Dog. The airplane setting also brought back memories of Whitaker’s first style icon. “My mom had the biggest influence on how I dress,” she says. “She had an incredible collection of vintage designer pieces and no matter the occasion, would serve a fit worth talking about.” Her mother wore heels on flights, a detail I thought about longer than I care to admit as someone who aspires to be that type of extra.

Whitaker has her own good heels, too. “I have a pair of dark red Prada velvet heels that I love to pull out for a good holiday party,” she says. I’d borrow that detail for a dressier take on the same outfit. Keep the jeans, swap the boots for a cheerful mood shoe, and let a sliver of color show beneath the hem. It’s just enough holiday for me, and I can guarantee those jeans would see more of January and the rest of 2027 than any sequin pants ever would.

title: Havilah Unique: From Foster Care to Creative Multi-hyphenate
text:
Havilah Unique: From Foster Care to Creative Multi-hyphenate

Havilah Unique ‪@havilah‬ is an unstoppable creative force. An entrepreneur, multidisciplinary artist, model, and content creator, Havilah has built a career chasing her creativity. From designing jewelry, furniture, and clothing (including the top she wore during our interview), Havilah’s creativity knows no bounds. But her path to becoming an entrepreneur and creative director was not easy. Growing up in North Providence, Havilah was raised in and out of the foster care system, taking on adult responsibilities at a very early age. She overcame incredible obstacles, including being raised apart from some of her siblings, meeting her father at 26, and being diagnosed with ADHD in elementary school.

During our conversation, Havilah spoke openly about how she learned to channel her symptoms into creative entrepreneurship. She was equally vulnerable about realizing she was burned out from her work, and the two-year sabbatical she took to center herself. Havilah offers us a look into how she learned to make choosing joy an intentional practice. We explore the rituals that help her feel her best, from her DIY hair and body care routines to how she prepares for a great night out. Havilah reflects on her sobriety journey, ceremonial smoking, offering us an honest look at what it takes to protect your energy while continuing to create. After meeting Brooke three years ago, the two finally sit down to talk about being archetypal Leo women, creativity, and the beauty of becoming.

title: How To Make Friends As a Busy Adult, According to OG Community-Builder Lala Romero
text:
How To Make Friends As a Busy Adult, According to OG Community-Builder Lala Romero

I really value friendship. To me, it’s the only relationship I know that gives and takes in equal measure. Friendships provide a home, a sanctuary, for us to be our fullest, messiest, and truest selves. It’s our friends who we call when we want to perrear the night away, book a trip to our motherland, or just gab and gobble down garlic bread. It’s also our friends who hold us when we’re heartbroken, drop off meds and sopita when we’re sick, and remind us of who we are when we dare to doubt ourselves in front of them.

Friendships nourish our hearts, minds, spirits, and even our bodies — and yet, unfortunately for us, we’re in the middle of a loneliness epidemic. According to the CDC, about 1 in 3 U.S. adults say they feel lonely. Meanwhile, the Pew Research Center found that nearly 1 in 5 adults don’t have any close friends. This means that millions of people are moving through their lives without connections that make them feel known, cared for, seen, heard, supported, and like they belong.

And I think this conversation about loneliness feels particularly urgent for Latinas. We’re living through a moment when so many people are carrying fear around immigration enforcement and family separation, worrying about their safety, or feeling the weight of financial stress. When you’re living with that level of anxiety, having people you can call, people who will show up, people who make you feel safe, people who you can still experience joy, laughter, and calm with, isn’t just comforting. It’s absolutely necessary. 

But how do you build that community? How do you create that home within homegirls? Especially when you’ve graduated from school, maybe work from home, are new to town, or are just a shy, timid girl who has trouble making eye contact? Maybe you do have friends, but you all live in different cities now or are transitioning into new roles as mothers or business owners that keep you, or them, busier than usual.

In a country divided, a culture starving for connection, and a time when so many of us are just trying to hold it all together, how the hell do we make friends? I’m glad you asked! In this week’s episode of Sin Vergüenza by Somos, we’re speaking with Lala Romero, founder and CEO of Bella Doña and professional community builder, about why it can feel so hard to build community as an adult, how she does it, and what it’s taught her about friendship.
